The Chain catshark Scyliorhinus retifer is a small, deep-dwelling elasmobranch found along the continental slope of the western Atlantic, where it inhabits depths typically exceeding seventy meters. Neonates emerge from their leathery egg cases at a total length of 10.6 centimeters [Lb = 10.6 centimeters], a size that reflects the modest yolk reserves allocated during a prolonged incubation that, at a constant temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], lasts approximately 256 days [ab = approximately 256 days]. This extended embryonic period is characteristic of many scyliorhinid sharks and is thought to be an adaptation to the cool, stable thermal conditions of their benthic habitat, where metabolism proceeds at a deliberate pace. Upon hatching, the young are fully independent, quickly dispersing into the surrounding rocky crevices to feed on small crustaceans and polychaetes. The protracted developmental time underscores a life-history strategy geared toward producing well-developed offspring capable of immediate foraging, a pattern that contrasts with the abbreviated embryonic phases seen in some shallow-water congeners and is reflective of an energetic trade-off between producing few, well-provisioned eggs rather than many smaller ones.

The onset of reproductive capability therefore emerges only after several years of sustained feeding and accumulation of bodily reserves, a conservative schedule that buffers against the uncertainties of deep-sea resource availability. Females tend to mature at slightly larger sizes than males, a dimorphism linked to the physical demands of carrying developing eggs.

Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight recorded for adult individuals is approximately 700 grams [Wwi = approximately 700 grams], a mass that represents the culmination of years of gradual tissue accretion. This relatively low body weight combined with a modest length gives the Chain catshark a slender, elongate profile, well suited for maneuvering through the complex benthic terrain of its habitat.
